UK patient transport · NEPTS sector intelligence packet · September 2026

A £0.5bn tender-allocated utility, consolidating toward two national independents — and the owner of the largest one should underwrite renewal rate, not journey growth.

One synthesis of five workstreams — the NHS England market baseline, the 2021–26 tender and award record across all 42 ICB areas, the competitor and failures ledger, the EMED contract book, and the add-on map — carried in the structure of a diligence package: decision, numbers, conditions and the ask, evidence, an outreach kit and a monitor board. Framed as sponsor-side commercial diligence — market structure, tender dynamics, competitor set, add-on targets — for a control owner three years into a platform build. The brief's "patient transportation" is cut to NHS non-emergency patient transport (NEPTS), the tendered, ICB-commissioned market where E-zec/EMED is the largest independent; secure mental-health transport and pathology logistics are flagged as the two adjacencies that pull through.

Six integrated takeaways

01

The moat is the KPI record, not the vehicle.

Commissioners buy renewal on evidence: BOB/Frimley weighted quality 40% and price 10%; Dorset 60/40; Kent 36/35.

02

Buyer and seller are consolidating in step.

42 ICBs became 26 leadership teams in 2025 and 36 entities in April 2026; two merged commissioners now have a single NEPTS provider

03

The trusts are exiting the South, not the North.

SCAS ceded Sussex, Surrey and Thames Valley; EMAS lost Derbyshire but took Lincolnshire back for ten years

04

Distress is the deal flow.

Bristol Ambulance EMS (CQC Outstanding) went into administration with assets sold to EMED the same day; Spark/Medi 4 pre-packed in February; the King's incumbent collapsed on six hours' notice.

05

Wages outrun uplifts; only scale absorbs the gap.

Labour is ~70% of cost. NLW rose 9.8%, 6.7% and 4.1% in three Aprils with employer NIC to 15%. Fixed envelopes (Sussex £23M/yr

06

HTG-UK is the competitor to model, not G4S.

Thames Ambulance Service renamed, owned by a social-infrastructure fund since 2021, holding five ICB areas after taking Dorset from E-zec (2023), Cornwall, Norfolk & Waveney and …

Part I — Decision · Recommendation and the record

This packet is written to be read by a deal team in one sitting and to survive being read a second time by the portfolio company's management.

1 · Recommendation

✔ PROCEED — with the add-on programme, narrowly, and with the North West bid decision gated

  • Secure mental-health transport roll-up — five to eight founder-owned SMEs at £2–8M each, folded into Safe Care, funded from facility headroom. Start now
  • Distressed regional NEPTS operators — a standing watchlist (§6.5) with pre-agreed administrator terms and a mobilisation team on standby. Event-driven
  • Pathology / courier bolt-ons — small, non-CQC, same depots; opportunistic.
  • The North West bid — proceed to a bid decision under the pre-registered rules in §9: lot 2 (GM + Glossop) first, lot 1 …
  • Resolve the two live Southern renewals — Shropshire (24-month option, term ended 30 Sep 2026) and the H&IoW lapse — before spring 2027.

Conditions: four absolute (#01 contract and indexation register · #02 KPI packs · #03 FY25/FY26 accounts by contract · #04 April uplift outcomes) before the next add-on cheque or the NW bid submission — §11.

✘ DECLINE — three things this packet recommends against, in writing

  • The HTG-UK combination at any frame in the next 24 months. A merger with CMA review at a combined share that would trouble …
  • A HATS process before the NW award. Two simultaneous mobilisations is the TASL 2017 pattern; the failures ledger is explicit about what it costs.
  • Diversification into event medical, demand-responsive transport, or the devolved nations. Different buyers, thin margins, closed markets

And one thing not to underwrite: the strong form of the "inflation-linked infrastructure" framing. Until the indexation clauses are read (#01/#04), every April is a commercial event, not a formula.

Q1 expanded — nine markers that the sector is being designed for incumbents

  1. Minimum turnover thresholds. Sussex required £23M (2023) — a bar equal to a regional SME's whole revenue. S14
  2. Term lengthening. NHSE advised ≥5 years in 2021; the 2024–26 cohort is 5+5 and 5+3 throughout; Lincolnshire is ten straight.
  3. PSR Process C. Eight direct-award renewals in 2024–26 without competition; the route exists only for an incumbent "satisfying the contract". S29 S30 S54
  4. Decarbonisation thresholds. 75% ULEV/ZEV on 2026 renewals, 100% by 2030 — a fleet-financing test, not an environmental one. S1
  5. Financial review of low bids. NHSE's anti-Coperforma rule — commissioners are told to test a low price before awarding it. S1
  6. Commissioner consolidation. 42 → 36 entities with wave 2 coming; merged ICBs inherit multiple providers and re-lot larger. S39 S63
  7. Lot inflation. North West £58M/yr; K&M £26.3M/yr; Sussex £23M/yr — each larger than the entire E-zec of 2021. S28 S27 S14
  8. Quality-weighted scoring. Price at 10–40% of the score; integration, access and social value can only be evidenced at scale. S16 S27 S55
  9. Trust retreat from the South. SCAS, LAS, SECAmb, SWASFT out of the tendered market; the only Southern in-house lot (H&IoW) has lapsed. S1 S54

§2.1 · Sizing — three methods, one range

There is no published national NEPTS spend series. The 2021 review built its £460M from CCG returns and provider surveys; NHS SBS, marketing a framework in 2026, cites "approximately £500 million". A third method

§2.2 · Demand anatomy — who travels, why, and what changes it

Demand and cost drivers — direction of travel · S1 S15 S39
DriverDirectionEvidenceRead for a control owner
Ageing populationUp75% of NEPTS users are over 65; ~1.45M over-65s find hospital travel difficult (Age UK/ILC)Structural volume support; acuity mix (stretcher, bariatric) rising — Sussex reports more specialist demand than forecast within a year of …
Renal universal commitmentUp2022 eligibility guidance: transport support for all in-centre haemodialysis journeys; a third of dialysis patients previously had noneAnchor, predictable, time-critical and KPI-visible (renal on-time is the metric HSJ reported for Surrey); home haemodialysis is the slow offset
Elective recovery and dischargeUpDischarge ~10.6% of journeys; trusts buy ad-hoc capacity to clear beds (UH Sussex paid £1.2M to one ad-hoc provider in 2022)Unplanned work carries premium pricing but is the KPI that fails first at mobilisation
Outpatient transformationDownNHSE targeted a 30% cut in face-to-face outpatients by 2023/24; modelled 10–15% fewer NEPTS journeys, ≥4% of resources releasedOutpatient share (43%) is the swing; renal and discharge insulate the block
Eligibility tighteningCost300,000–500,000 unsuccessful applications a year; ~70% of appeals succeed (Healthwatch Northumberland); PTAC/single-point-of-access models decideThe co-ordination hub is where eligibility is decided — owning it protects block volume and controls sub-contract spend
Cancellations and abortsCost~25% of bookings cancelled or aborted (~3M/yr) — hospital cancellations the largest single causeThe utilisation lever — dispatch technology, hospital integration and abort compensation clauses, not headcount
ICB budgets and structurePressureICB running costs cut 50% (2025); 'strategic commissioner' model; NEPTS <0.5% of NHS spend and historically under-managed (review: 'lack of …Thin commissioners lean on incumbents and direct awards — an incumbency tailwind with an eligibility-tightening tail

§2.3 · Unit economics — the vehicle-day, illustrated

No provider publishes contract-level economics. The public record does allow a bounded illustration: NHSE puts labour at ~70% of cost and 73% of journeys on single-crewed vehicles; EMAS reports 120 vehicles delivering ~20,000 journeys a month (~7–8 per vehicle-day on a 22-day month)

Illustrative vehicle-day economics — CreditSwan arithmetic on public inputs; every cell is an assumption to be replaced by dispatch and payroll data
Line (per vehicle-day, 10-hour shift)Single-crew car / WAVTwo-crew stretcher ambulanceBasis
Journeys delivered6–84–6EMAS 7–8/vehicle-day; Sussex 5–6/staff-day; stretcher work is longer and often two-way with waits
Revenue yield per journey£45–60£90–140Independents' blended yield £60–70 (derived, §5.7); stretcher/bariatric/HDU priced above; taxi/car below
Revenue per vehicle-day£300–430£450–700product of the two rows
Crew cost (loaded)£165–190£330–380NLW £12.71 → ~£13.50 base for ACA + 30% on-costs (NIC 15%, pension, holiday, training) ≈ £17–19/hr × 10 h
Vehicle (lease, fuel, maintenance, insurance)£40–60£100–140car/WAV vs converted 3.5 t ambulance; EV transition raises lease, lowers fuel
Control room, eligibility, management, estate£45–65 (15%)£70–105 (15%)NHSE four-component model; shared across the fleet
Contribution per vehicle-day£25–115−£60 to +£75wide because journeys/day and yield dominate
Contribution as % of revenue8–27%−13% to +11%single-crew cars make the margin; two-crew ambulances make the KPI
What the arithmetic says

Three levers move contribution more than price does: journeys per vehicle-day (utilisation — the abort rate is the enemy), crew mix (the 73% single-crew share is where margin lives

§2.4 · The wage clock

§2.5 · The April bridge — uplift minus wage, in margin points

The published contract envelopes are fixed sums (Sussex £23M a year; Kent & Medway £210.7M over eight years; BOB/F £222.6M over ten).

The April 2027 bridge — illustrative, CreditSwan arithmetic; replace with the indexation clause register and payroll
Contract uplift securedRevenue effectLabour cost effect (5.0–5.5% on £133M)NetMargin effect (bps on £190M)
0% (fixed block, no uplift)£0+£6.7–7.3M−£6.7–7.3M−350 to −385 bps
2%+£3.8M+£6.7–7.3M−£2.9–3.5M−150 to −185 bps
3%+£5.7M+£6.7–7.3M−£1.0–1.6M−55 to −85 bps
4% (full labour pass-through)+£7.6M+£6.7–7.3M+£0.3–0.9M+15 to +45 bps
Utilisation offset needed at 2% uplift——1.5–1.8% of coste.g. abort rate 25% → 22%, or +0.3 journeys per vehicle-day
The clause register answers it — six fixed, five cost-factor, one wage-indexed

The contract register (D1–D12) shows six fixed-envelope contracts (39% of contract revenue), five referencing an NHS cost-uplift factor and one wage-indexed (LLR); April 2026 uplifts ran 1.8–3.4% against a 4.6% wage line. Before the register we did not know

§2.6 · The fleet clock — decarbonisation as a threshold, not a cost line

Decarbonisation — scope, assumptions and effect
ItemWhat the record saysImplication
ScopeTargets apply to the aggregate fleet used on a contract or lead-provider arrangement, including sub-contractors on dynamic frameworksThe lead provider is accountable for its taxi and community-transport partners' fleets — another reason the hub matters
AmbulancesExcluded from the 2035 date; NHSE to set an ambulance trajectory later; LAS and WMAS piloting electric emergency ambulancesTwo-crew stretcher fleets have longer runway; cars, WAVs and minibuses do not
Cost assumptionsEV purchase/lease parity 'by 2030 or earlier'; fuel and maintenance savings per DfT TAG; public charging expansionProviders renewing in 2026–27 buy before parity; capex is front-loaded against five-year terms
Evidence of adoptionDocGo UK ran six electric NEPTS ambulances with Stockport FT (2023); G4S/Fraikin 162 modular 3.5 t vehicles on contract hire for Kent (2026)Contract hire, not ownership, is the sector's answer to threshold risk
Threshold effectA £5M-turnover SME with 40 vehicles cannot finance a 75% ULEV fleet on a five-year contract without an owner's balance …Decarbonisation is a consolidation mechanism as much as an environmental one

§2.7 · Regulation — two regimes, one moat

Regulatory architecture — what governs a NEPTS contract
RegimeMechanicsEffect on competition
CQC registrationCarrying patients in a vehicle designed or modified for the purpose is the regulated activity 'transport services, triage and medical …Ratings are award criteria in all but name (BAEMS Outstanding; TASL/HTG-UK Requires Improvement at Canvey 2023; TASL lost N.
Provider Selection Regime (Jan 2024)NEPTS sits inside PSR, not the Procurement Act 2023. Direct Award A (only one capable provider), B (patient choice), C …Incumbency is the asset: Hillingdon (HATS), Birmingham & Solihull (£42M), Greater Manchester (£17.5M), NENC, South Yorkshire, Humber and H&IoW (SCAS …
NHS Standard ContractMandatory contract form; service conditions require data sharing for the national dataset; KPIs and remedial notices are localStandardised terms lower switching cost for commissioners — the specification, not the contract form, is where providers differentiate
National eligibility criteria (2022)Medical need, cognitive/sensory impairment, significant mobility need, safeguarding; universal renal commitment; expectation of independent travel otherwiseConsistency reduces the eligibility 'grey area' but hands the decision to the hub
TransparencyNational minimum dataset intended from 2022 (volumes, waits, journey times by type); publication cadence six-monthlyA published KPI league table would price renewals nationally; its absence keeps performance local and negotiable
Procurement advice (NHSE 2021)Specialist contracts ≥5 years; fixed block + variation; ≥60 working days to bid; activity data for two prior yearsCodified reasons to prefer capitalised bidders; the 'financial review of low bids' clause is the anti-Coperforma rule

§2.8 · Devolved nations and the English exception

Scotland (Scottish Ambulance Service, 400K+ patient transport journeys a year), Wales (WAST NEPTS, ~700K journeys with a large volunteer-car component) and Northern Ireland (NIAS) provide patient transport inside their national ambulance services. Independents appear only as sub-contract capacity

What we recommend against

Modelling volume growth. The national journey count has been flat at 11–12M for a decade of policy documents; outpatient transformation and home dialysis push down while ageing and discharge push up. Underwrite share and yield, not market growth.

§3.9 · A national framework in the wings — NHS LPP

NHS London Procurement Partnership (hosted by Guy's and St Thomas') issued a PIN in November 2025 for a national NEPTS framework under the PSR competitive process

What has changed since the 2021 review — and what has not

Changed. PSR replaced the light-touch Public Contracts Regulations regime (Jan 2024); direct awards became the Northern default; terms lengthened to 5+5 and 5+3 as NHSE advised; thresholds appeared (Sussex £23M); commissioners merged; the trusts left the South.

What we recommend against

Reading a direct award as a renewal. Process C awards observed in 2025–26 are 6–24 month bridges (GM, SY, B&S, NENC) — placeholders for full processes, not ten-year commitments.

17.4 · The NHS LPP national NEPTS framework — a new route to market

What it is

NHS London Procurement Partnership (hosted by Guy's and St Thomas') issued a PIN in November 2025 for a national Non-Emergency Patient Transport Services framework under the PSR competitive process, with a market-engagement event on 1 December 2025.

The framework's anticipated lots — S67 · lot structure may change
Framework lot (anticipated)What it coversEMED positionCompetitors likely on the lot
Core NEPTStandard planned and on-day transport, all mobilities, 24/7The core business; national coverage from 60+ basesHTG-UK, G4S, HATS, DocGo, DHL, regional SMEs
RenalDialysis transport — three sessions a week, time-criticalRenal is the anchor in every EMED contractSame set; SMEs with renal-unit relationships
SecureMental-health and secure conveyanceSafe Care division; HPFT, SABP, Sussex specSecure Care UK, Secure24, EAMC, Elite — the add-on long-list
High DependencyTwo-crew, clinically staffed transfersHDU capability; BAEMS critical-care contractAmbulance trusts, DocGo, specialist independents
ResilienceSurge, emergency step-in, provider failure coverThe BAEMS and Sussex mobilisation record is the evidenceHATS (King's precedent), G4S, HTG-UK
What we recommend against

Treating the six new CEOs as continuity. Three of them (Central East, Surrey & Sussex, West & North London) are new to their footprint; the contracts they inherit were signed by people who no longer hold the pen.

Valuation reference points — and their limits

No UK NEPTS transaction in the sources discloses an EBITDA multiple. The two reference points are indirect: Real Assets IM's €200–250M (press) for the whole of HTG in 2021 — ~7,000 staff and 2,800 ambulances, predominantly Spanish concessions

What we recommend against

Modelling G4S as the marginal competitor. It has retained one region for a decade and shown no appetite for others; HTG-UK has won five in three years.

18.3 · Why London is different — and why it has not been consolidated

London vs the rest — why the nationals are not there yet
FactorLondonRest of EnglandImplication for entry
BuyerTrusts (30+), each with its own contract, since LAS left in 2017ICBs, one lot per footprintNo single tender to win; the framework or the merged ICB is the first aggregation point
Journey profileShort, dense, congested; high renal and oncology load; low car ownership; many inter-site transfers within trust groupsLonger rural journeys; car and volunteer schemes viableVehicle utilisation is higher but on-time performance is harder; congestion pricing (ULEZ) already forces ULEV fleets
WorkforceLondon Living Wage expectations; higher turnover; competition from LAS, private hire and logistics for driversNLW-anchoredThe wage bridge is steeper in London — an unindexed contract fails faster
EstateDepots scarce and expensive; SEND day-books (HATS) fund vehicle utilisationDepots cheap; no SEND cross-subsidyA London entrant needs either an acquired depot network (HATS) or a partner
PoliticalTrust boards and the London regional team; the merged W&NL ICB is new and largeICB-ledThe ICB-wide lot decision is a 2027–29 event; the framework may pre-empt it
Providers presentG4S, HATS, DHL, SVL, DocGo remnants, SMEsEMED, HTG-UK, trustsThe two nationals are absent; whoever enters first at ICB scale sets the reference

18.4 · Entry routes — ranked

Entry routes — the framework first, HATS later, the ICB-wide lot as the prize
RouteHowCost and timeFit with the packet's recommendation
1 · The LPP frameworkBid every lot (Core, Renal, Secure, HDU, Resilience) when the competitive process is published; use the Resilience lot as the London entryBid cost only; no mobilisation until a call-offConsistent — no bandwidth conflict with the NW; the Secure lot doubles as the Safe Care platform's national route
2 · HATSBilateral approach after the NW award; a partnership for London lots as the alternativeThe largest cheque after HTG-UK; a 2028 conversationRecommended timing: after NW and the BOB/F–Sussex records (Decision §1)
3 · Trust-level wins as contracts expireUCLH/RNOH, Royal Free, LNWH and SEL contracts roll 2027–29; PSR Process C favours incumbents, so the route is a competitive …Small contracts (£2–7M/yr); mobilisation without a depot networkOpportunistic; only where a depot exists (BAEMS-type acquisition of a London SME would supply one)
4 · The West & North London ICB-wide lotIf the merged ICB moves from trust contracts to one lot (as every other Southern ICB has), the first London-scale …Unknown timing; likely 2028–30The prize; the framework and HATS are the two ways to be positioned for it
5 · Distressed London SMEsThe SVL/King's pattern — a London operator failing on working capital; the watchlist (§6.5) with London depots as the targetEvent-drivenConsistent; supplies the depot the other routes lack
What we recommend against

Bidding London trust contracts one at a time without a depot. The mobilisation cost of a £3M/yr trust contract in central London exceeds its first-year contribution

§5.7 · Revenue and margin — method, not a number

The ledger closes the range — £188.4M FY26 revenue, £15.6M EBITDA

The billing ledger and GL (D1–D12) put FY26 revenue at £188.4M and EBITDA at £15.6M (8.3%) — inside the derived range and above Method B, because Patient Care yield is £74 a journey, not £60–70. Method A

Illustrative — CreditSwan arithmetic; the FY25 filing due Sep 2026 and management accounts replace every row
Illustrative P&L stack (FY26, £M)LowHighBasis
Revenue170210Methods A and B
Staff costs (≈70%)119147NHSE cost structure; 4,000 colleagues at £30–37K loaded
Fleet (lease, fuel, maintenance, insurance) (≈12–15%)20321,400+ vehicles; £14–23K per vehicle-year
Estate, control rooms, IT, insurance, overhead (≈8–10%)142160+ bases; Cleric/CAD; clinical governance
EBITDA (residual)12–1715–267–8% low case; 9–12% high case — bracketed by the vehicle-day arithmetic in §2.3
Sensitivity: each 1% of uplift not passed through−1.2−1.570% labour × 1% on revenue
How do we know the margin band is plausible?

We do not know it; we bound it. The vehicle-day arithmetic (§2.3) gives 8–27% contribution on single-crew work and negative-to-low-teens on two-crew, which at a 73:27 mix and after central costs lands high-single-digit EBITDA for a mobilising national operator.

§5.8 · Strengths and vulnerabilities — from outside

Strengths on the record

  • Scale and contiguity. 15 ICB areas from the Thames Valley to Nottinghamshire; 60+ bases
  • Commissioner alignment after the mergers. Sole NEPTS provider to NHS Surrey and Sussex and to NHS Thames Valley; the largest provider inside Central East.
  • A stabilisation record. Sussex: six months to business-as-usual, complaints −70%, 85.65% call answer — in the commissioner's own words.
  • Adjacent divisions already exist. Safe Care, Courier and Community Care give the roll-up a home; secure MH is bundled into Surrey and Sussex specifications.
  • Distress conversion proven. BAEMS: assets, staff, depots and a BNSSG contract on the day of administration.
  • Refinanced before sale. Glas Trust facility (Mar 2025) — capacity for add-ons is a question of headroom, not of a new process.

Vulnerabilities on the record

  • Surrey 2024. A nationally reported KPI shortfall on the first ex-SCAS contract; the recovery trajectory is not public.
  • The 2029–30 wall. Four of the five largest contracts expire in 14 months
  • Two losses to the same rival. Dorset (2023) and Suffolk (2026) to HTG-UK — the duopoly is competitive, not settled.
  • Legacy terms are opaque. Seven E-zec-era areas with no published term; Shropshire at term now; H&W by 2027.
  • Labour exposure. 4,000 colleagues, 470 recently TUPE'd from an NHS trust with pension direction; NLW-anchored pay
  • Political visibility. The largest PE-owned NHS transport contractor under a government led by a former Health Secretary who championed "NHS preferred provider".
What we recommend against

Quoting a revenue or EBITDA number for EMED. The packet gives a range and a method; the FY25 filing is weeks away. Quote the method.

19.5 · The bridge, worked — three contract archetypes

The same April lands differently depending on the clause. The table works April 2027 for a £23M/yr contract (the Sussex envelope) at 70% labour, with a 5.0% blended labour-cost increase (NLW ~4%, AfC round on the transferee cohort, NIC and …

The bridge by archetype — illustrative; the clause register (#01) says which archetype each EMED contract is
ArchetypeHow the uplift worksApril 2027 uplift on £23MCost increaseNetMargin effect
A · Fixed envelope, negotiated upliftThe published total is the contract; any uplift is a variation the commissioner may decline0–2% → £0–0.46M£16.1M × 5.0% + £6.9M × 3% = £1.01M−£0.55M to −£1.01M−240 to −440 bps
B · Annual uplift linked to an NHS cost factorThe clause references the NHS Payment Scheme cost-uplift factor or a published index≈ 2.5–3.5% → £0.58–0.81M£1.01M−£0.20M to −£0.43M−85 to −185 bps
C · Wage-indexed (NLW / AfC pass-through) with a capThe labour share moves with the statutory rates; non-labour with CPI; often capped≈ 4.4% → £1.01M£1.01M≈ £0≈ 0 bps
Utilisation offset available in any archetypeAbort rate 25% → 22%; +0.3 journeys per vehicle-day; single-crew share up 2 pts—−£0.35–0.50M of cost+150–220 bpsThe operating answer to archetype A
What a good uplift clause looks like — the diligence test

Three features, in descending order of value: (1) an index rather than a negotiation — the NHS Payment Scheme cost-uplift factor, CPI or a wage index named in the contract

What we recommend against

Modelling labour at a single rate. Two clocks (LPC and AfC), two cohorts (transferees and new hires), and a pension differential of twenty points make the blended rate a function of mix and time, not a number.

A North West win does not fix an unindexed Southern book; it adds £17M of revenue at 5% in year one to a business whose margin is set elsewhere.

§7 · The infrastructure thesis — bull, bear and the re-test

Tiger describes EMED as an outsourced NHS contractor on "long-term, inflation-linked contracts" (S9)

The thesis, stated fairly, then tested

Strong form: NEPTS is essential-service infrastructure — regulated, long-dated, inflation-protected, with a demand base (renal, ageing, discharge) that cannot be switched off and a buyer that cannot walk away. Weak form: NEPTS is a labour-services business whose contract structure …

§7.1 · Limb by limb

The strong-form thesis, tested against the public record
ClaimEvidence forEvidence againstVerdict
Essential serviceStatutory duty on ICBs to secure NEPTS; universal renal commitment; 20,000 users every weekdayEligibility is discretionary at the margin (300–500K refusals a year); outpatient volume can be designed out (30% F2F target)Supported — for renal, discharge and mobility-need cohorts; not for the outpatient swing
Long-datedNHSE advice: ≥5 years for specialist provision; 5+5 (Sussex, BOB/F, SNEE, Surrey, LLR), 5+3 (K&M, NW, Dorset), 10 straight (Lincolnshire)Initial terms are five years; extensions are the commissioner's option, exercised on record; four of EMED's five largest contracts expire in one 14-month windowPartly — long if renewed; the renewal is earned, not owned
Inflation-linkedNHS Standard Contract allows uplifts; commissioners have historically funded NLW pressure in social care and some NEPTS renegotiationsNo notice publishes an indexation formula; envelopes are fixed sums (Sussex £23M/yr; K&M £210.7M/8y); NHSE recommends volume variation, not priceNot evidenced — the claim to verify, not to rely on
Regulated barrierCQC registration for purpose-built vehicles; ~296 registered providers, only four with an ICB lot; 75%→100% ULEV/ZEV; £23M turnover thresholds; 60-day bidsRegistration is cheap and common (300 providers); the barrier is capital and evidence, not licenceSupported — as a scale barrier rather than a regulatory one
Uncontestable positionEMED ~3× the nearest pure-play; sole provider to two merged commissioners; trusts have exited the SouthSCAS lost three lots in one cycle; EMED lost Dorset and Suffolk to HTG-UK; EMAS re-entered Lincolnshire for ten years; Kent drew seven biddersNot supported — contestable at every term
Demand growthAgeing; renal universal offer; discharge pressure; Sussex acuity above forecastNational journeys flat at 11–12M across a decade of policy; outpatient transformation; home dialysis; eligibility tighteningFlat volume, rising acuity — underwrite mix and share, not growth
Buyer cannot walk awayICBs must secure provision; failures are bridged within days; in-house capacity in the South has been dismantled (SCAS TUPE'd 470 …EMAS shows a trust can rebuild in-house provision; a policy turn to "NHS preferred provider" would make it a templateTrue today; policy-dependent

§7.2 · Bull and bear

Bear case — the thesis is overstated

  • Rebid attrition is normal. SCAS lost Surrey, Thames Valley and Sussex in one cycle; EMAS lost Derbyshire; HTG lost LLR; E-zec lost Dorset; EMED lost Suffolk.
  • Wages outrun uplifts. Labour ~70% of cost; NLW +9.8%/+6.7%/+4.1%; employer NIC to 15%; NHS Pension direction for TUPE cohorts.
  • Mobilisation is where reputations die. Surrey 2024 KPI failures were reported nationally; Coperforma collapsed in weeks; the King's incumbent gave six hours' notice.
  • Buyers are shrinking and poorer. ICB running costs −50%; merged commissioners will re-lot; eligibility can be tightened by guidance
  • Political tail. A new government (PM Burnham, July 2026; Health Secretary Yvette Cooper) with an "NHS preferred provider" history
  • The duopoly is competitive. HTG-UK has an infra owner, a young fleet and two wins against EMED; the NW is its opportunity to double.
  • Volume drift. Virtual outpatients (43% of journeys are outpatient) and home dialysis erode the swing volume over a decade.

What would prove the bear right

Loss of any 2025-cohort contract at 2030; two consecutive Aprils with uplift below NLW by more than 3 points; a CQC downgrade at a flagship; PSR guidance steering NEPTS to in-house provision; HTG-UK winning two NW lots.

Bull case — the thesis is right in substance

  • PSR incumbency. Direct Award Process C has become the Northern default
  • Thresholds and terms design out the tail. £23M minimum turnover, 5+5 terms, 75%→100% ULEV/ZEV, financial review of low bids: the market is being …
  • Distress is share. One failure a year on average; a prepared buyer with commissioner trust converts each into contracts and crews on the day …
  • Anchor demand is statutory. Universal renal transport commitment; 75% of users over 65; discharge pressure is a system priority.
  • Trusts have retreated where the money is. The South East and Midlands are now private markets
  • Scale wins quality scoring. Quality, integration and access are 55–90% of award weightings; only a national operator can evidence them across every criterion.
  • Two merged commissioners already have one provider. EMED (Surrey & Sussex, Thames Valley) — and the PSR makes that a renewal route.

What would prove the bull right

Direct-award extensions on Surrey/LLR at 2029; NW lot won or shared; uplift clauses that reference NHS cost-uplift factors; secure-MH add-ons closing at low multiples; Shropshire extended without a process.

One. This is a portfolio-owner request, not a sale process: the purpose is to replace derived ranges with company figures before capital is committed to add-ons or a bid. Two. The four Tier 1 items are files that exist

§13 · Commissioner and operator outreach kit — ready to run; the decision is Tiger's

A stratified 28-interview programme that converts the public record into first-hand evidence on renewal intentions, the North West, secure-MH buying and the distressed pipeline

Decision banner

Whether to contact anyone, who conducts the calls, and prior counsel review are entirely the deal team's decisions.

Sample
28
targets across eight strata; 25–30 band; substitution rule below
Duration
3 weeks
two callers; ~4 calls a day; one-page synthesis per stratum
Primary question
Renewal
what the five EMED-area commissioners intend at 2029–30 and what they think of the record
Secondary
North West
how the ITT is being designed and who is expected to bid

13.1 · The frame and why it is stratified this way

Two populations answer two different questions. Commissioners and trusts answer the renewal question — they hold the +5 options, they wrote the HOSC paper, they will design the Surrey–Sussex lot. Operators, alumni, practitioners and unions answer the market question

0 · Introduction and consent2Who is calling and for whom (counsel-approved script); purpose (understanding the NEPTS market for an owner of a provider; no representations); voluntarySame

  4. North West bidBid team, lot strategy, price-quality positioning under the NHS SBS process, and exposure to legal challenge (two challenges halted the last …

How a signal escalates

Four stages, separated on purpose — the thing that detects never edits the thesis
StageWhat happensOwner

3 · RecommendA written action — a data request, a commissioner conversation, a bid-rule check, a re-run of the §7 gridEMED exec / Tiger deal lead
4 · ActThe action is executed and the packet is re-issued if a hypothesis verdict changesAs assigned
What the monitors replace

Before this cadence the sector is reviewed when someone has a reason to look — in practice after a lost tender or a press story.

Recommendation

Sector: Attractive for a scaled incumbent, unattractive for a new entrant. NEPTS rewards the incumbent with the deepest KPI record, the widest territory inside merging commissioner boundaries, and the balance sheet to carry decarbonisation and mobilisation. It punishes new entrants and sub-scale operators

How to read the scorecard

Yield and utilisation move in opposite directions across the book — the stretcher-heavy South East contracts price highest (£74–81) and run the fewest journeys per vehicle-day (5.3–5.7); Staffordshire runs 6.9 at £55. That is acuity mix, not management. The two columns to read together are discharge and call answer: both are hospital-facing, and both slip on the same contract in the same weeks.

§21.2 · Utilisation — the vehicle-day, read weekly

What the abort line is worth

The April 2027 table in §2.5 needs a 1.5–1.8% cost offset at a 2% uplift — an abort rate moving from 25% to 22%. The book is at 22.8% and the trend is down; the offset is two-thirds delivered on the dispatch data. The remaining third is hospital cancellations, and that is a contract-clause and integration question, not a dispatch one.

What we recommend against

Reading a watch as a trip, or moving a threshold to make one go away. Seven monitors are on watch because the calendar is busy, not because the operation has deteriorated; five of them are external and will resolve on other people's decisions. The two Surrey KPIs are the ones that carry money — and the discharge threshold that tripped this week was written in June, when the contract was clearing it.

What the monitors replace

Before this cadence the sector was reviewed when someone had a reason to look — in practice after a lost tender or a press story. On the twelve weeks above, three signals would otherwise have surfaced at the next monthly KPI pack or later: the abort spike would have shown as a variable-revenue miss in the July accounts; the agency drift on BOB/F as a Q3 payroll variance; and the Surrey discharge slide in the commissioner's five-year plan, written by someone else. The Monday run reads them a month earlier and puts a named owner on each.

What re-issues the packet

A hypothesis verdict moves only on a written re-test. Two are exposed to this board: H4 (mobilisation record supports direct-award renewal) falls to 'confirmed for four of six' if Surrey discharge is not back above specification for four consecutive weeks by 5 October; H6 (partial pass-through) improves if the four fixed-envelope reopener responses arrive above 3%. Either re-issues Part I and the §7 grid; nothing else on this tab does.

The honest valuation statement

The sector is priced privately, deal by deal, and the only observable comparable is a concession-style Spanish platform sold to an infrastructure buyer. What can be said is directional: a book that indexes and renews by direct award is priced as infrastructure

What we recommend against

Planning the exit around the wall's date. Plan it around the extension decisions (2028–29) — those are the events that decide which side of the wall the sale lands on.

§A · Methodology and basis of preparation

Nine steps · public record only · no target data room, management interviews or expert calls
StepWhat was doneOutput
1 · BaselineRead the NHS England NEPTS review (Aug 2021) in full for market size, journey mix, cost structure, provider count, decarbonisation timeline and procurement advice§2 market baseline; F1–F4
2 · Contract recordPulled every NEPTS notice found on Find a Tender, Contracts Finder and Bidstats for 2021–26 (awards, intentions to award, DA-C, VEAT, modifications)§3.4 ledger; §3.5 map; annualised-value, coverage and calendar exhibits
3 · Commissioner mapMapped the 42 ICB footprints to providers using notices, ICB and trust pages and provider sites; graded each row§3.1 merger map; §3.5; F8–F9
4 · ProvidersBuilt profiles from company releases, sites, Companies House name histories and charges, CQC reports and press§4; F10–F12
5 · EMEDAssembled the arc, footprint, contract book, performance record and capital structure from Cairngorm, Arrowpoint, Gowling, Business Sale Report, EMED's site …§5; F13–F16
6 · Add-onsIdentified lanes from the contract record (secure-MH call-offs), the failures ledger (distressed operators) and provider profiles§6; F17
7 · ThesisTested Tiger's stated framing limb by limb against steps 1–5; assigned scenario probabilities by judgement§7; F18
8 · WatchboardConverted every unresolved item into a trigger, a live event, a monitor or a diligence request with a tier§8; F19–F20
9 · ReconciliationLogged every conflicting figure and resolved it in writing rather than averaging (§B)Appendix
Conventions
ConventionRule applied
AnnualisationPublished total ÷ maximum term including extensions (e.g. K&M £210.7M ÷ 8 = £26.3M/yr).
JourneysLatest disclosed annual figure per provider; monthly figures × 12 only where stated as a run-rate; pro-forma sums labelled.
Currency and tax£ sterling; contract values ex-VAT as published; € for the HTG transaction as reported.
DatesContract dates as in notices; ICB footprints pre-1 Apr 2026 for the map, post-merger for the commissioner table.
Confidenceverified (public record/filing) · external (company statement) · press · derived (CreditSwan arithmetic) · inferred (stated basis)
EstimatesShown with method and range; never a point; replaced by filings when available (EMED FY25 due Sep 2026).

§D · Glossary

TermMeaning in this packet
NEPTSNon-emergency patient transport services — NHS-funded transport for patients whose medical condition or mobility prevents independent travel to treatment.
ICB / ICSIntegrated care board — the statutory NHS commissioner (42 in 2022; 36 from Apr 2026); integrated care system — the wider partnership.
PSRProvider Selection Regime (Health Care Services (PSR) Regulations 2023, in force Jan 2024).
DA-C / DAP-CDirect Award Process C under PSR — renewal without competition to an existing provider.
Block / variableNHSE-recommended payment model: a fixed block for specialist provision with variation mechanisms when activity moves beyond thresholds
CQCCare Quality Commission — regulator; NEPTS in purpose-built vehicles is the regulated activity 'transport services, triage and medical advice provided …
TUPETransfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) — staff transfer with terms on contract change
NLWNational Living Wage — statutory floor for 21+; £12.71 from Apr 2026.
ULEV / ZEVUltra-low / zero-emission vehicle — thresholds in NEPTS contracts (75% from 2026, 100% from 2030, 100% ZEV 2035).
HTCSHealthcare Travel Costs Scheme — reimbursement for low-income patients; £5–10M/yr, outside NEPTS contracts.
PTAC / single point of accessPatient Transport Advice Centre — the co-ordination hub that assesses eligibility and books journeys
HDUHigh-dependency unit transport — two-crew, clinically staffed inter-hospital transfers; higher yield than core NEPTS.
s.136 / MHAMental Health Act powers under which patients are detained or conveyed; secure transport is a specialist adjacency.
ACVAnnual contract value.
